title: Part 5, Chapter 5
paragraphs: Lebeziatnikov looked agitated.

"I've come to see you, Sofya Semyonovna," he began. "Excuse me... I thought I'd find you here," he said, suddenly turning to Raskolnikov. "That is, I didn't mean anything like... But I just thought... Katerina Ivanovna has gone insane," he blurted out, turning back to Sonia.
Sonia screamed.

"At least it seems that way. But... we don't know what to do, you see! She came back — apparently she'd been thrown out somewhere, maybe beaten... At least that's what it looks like... She'd run to your father's old boss, but he wasn't home — he was dining at some other general's... Just imagine: she rushed off there, to the other general's, and she was so persistent that she got the boss called out from dinner, it seems. You can imagine what happened. She was thrown out, of course; but according to her own account, she screamed abuse at him and threw something at him. It's easy enough to believe... How she wasn't arrested, I can't understand! Now she's telling everyone, including Amalia Ivanovna — though it's hard to understand her; she's screaming and thrashing about... Oh yes, she's shouting that since everyone has abandoned her, she'll take the children into the street with a barrel organ, and the children will sing and dance, and she will too, and they'll collect money, and they'll go every day and stand under the general's window... 'to let everyone see well-born children, whose father was an official, begging in the streets.' She keeps hitting the children and they're all crying. She's teaching Lida to sing 'My Village,' the boy to dance, Polenka the same. She's ripping up all their clothes to make little caps like actors wear; she plans to carry a tin pan and bang on it instead of music... She won't listen to anything... Imagine what it's like! It's beyond anything!"

Lebeziatnikov would have gone on, but Sonia, who had been listening almost breathlessly, snatched up her cloak and hat and ran from the room, dressing as she went. Raskolnikov followed, and Lebeziatnikov came after.

"She's definitely lost her mind!" he said to Raskolnikov as they went into the street. "I didn't want to frighten Sofya Semyonovna, so I said 'it seems like it,' but there's no doubt about it. They say in consumption the tubercles sometimes reach the brain; I wish I knew more about medicine. I tried to reason with her, but she wouldn't listen."
"You talked to her about the tubercles?"

"Not exactly about the tubercles. Besides, she wouldn't have understood! But what I'm saying is, if you convince someone through logic that they have nothing to cry about, they'll stop crying. That's obvious. Don't you agree?"
"Life would be too easy if that were true," Raskolnikov answered.

"Excuse me, but of course it would be rather difficult for Katerina Ivanovna to understand. But did you know that in Paris they've been conducting serious experiments on the possibility of curing the insane through logical argument alone? A professor there — a respected scientist who recently died — believed such treatment was possible. His idea was that there's nothing really wrong with the insane person's body; insanity is, so to speak, a logical mistake, an error of judgment, an incorrect way of seeing things. He would gradually show the patient their error, and — would you believe it? — they say he was successful! But since he also used cold showers, how much of the success was due to the argument is unclear... At least, so it seems."

Raskolnikov had long since stopped listening. Reaching the building where he lived, he nodded to Lebeziatnikov and went in at the gate. Lebeziatnikov snapped out of his monologue, looked around, and hurried on.

Raskolnikov went into his tiny room and stood still in the middle of it. Why had he come back here? He looked at the yellowed, tattered wallpaper, the dust, the sofa... From the courtyard came a loud, persistent hammering — someone seemed to be banging nails. He went to the window, rose on tiptoe, and stared out into the yard for a long time, as if completely absorbed. But the yard was empty, and he couldn't see who was making the noise. In the building to the left, some windows were open; on the sills sat pots of sickly geraniums. Laundry hung from the windows... He knew it all by heart. He turned away and sat down on the sofa.
Never, never had he felt so terrifyingly alone!
Yes, he felt again that he might actually come to hate Sonia, now that he had made her more miserable.
"Why had he gone to her to beg for her tears? Why did he need to poison her life? How contemptible!"
"I'll stay alone," he decided firmly, "and she won't come to the prison!"
Five minutes later he looked up with a strange smile. It was a strange thought.
"Perhaps Siberia really would be better," he thought suddenly.

He couldn't have said how long he sat there, vague thoughts drifting through his mind. Then the door opened and Dunya came in. At first she stood still in the doorway and looked at him, just as he had stood looking at Sonia. Then she came in and sat down across from him, in the same chair as yesterday. He looked at her silently, almost blankly.
"Don't be angry, brother. I've only come for a minute," Dunya said.
Her expression was thoughtful but not severe. Her eyes were bright and soft. He could see she had come to him with love.

"Brother, now I know everything — everything. Dmitri Prokofitch has explained it all. They're harassing and persecuting you based on a stupid, contemptible suspicion... Dmitri Prokofitch told me there's no danger and that you shouldn't look at it with such horror. I don't think so either, and I completely understand how outraged you must be — and I'm afraid this outrage may leave a permanent mark on you. That's what worries me. As for your pulling away from us, I won't judge you — I don't dare — and forgive me for blaming you before. I feel that if I had such a burden, I too would withdraw from everyone. I won't say anything to Mother about this, but I'll talk about you constantly and tell her you'll come soon. Don't worry about her — I'll put her mind at ease. But don't push her too far either — come at least once. Remember, she's your mother. I've come simply to say" — Dunya started to get up — "that if you ever need me, for anything at all... call me, and I'll come. Goodbye!"
She turned sharply and headed for the door.
"Dunya!" Raskolnikov stopped her and walked toward her. "That Razumikhin — Dmitri Prokofitch — is a very good man."
Dunya blushed slightly.
"Well?" she asked, waiting a moment.
"He's capable, hardworking, honest, and capable of real love... Goodbye, Dunya."
Dunya blushed crimson, then suddenly looked alarmed.
"What do you mean, brother? Are we really parting forever — that you're giving me such a farewell message?"
"Never mind... Goodbye."
He turned away and went to the window. She stood there a moment, looked at him anxiously, and left, troubled.

No, he wasn't cold toward her. There had been one moment — the very last — when he had desperately wanted to take her in his arms and say goodbye to her, even to tell her, but he hadn't dared even to touch her hand.
"Afterward she might shudder remembering I embraced her, and feel I stole her kiss."
"And could she endure the truth?" he wondered a few minutes later. "No, she couldn't. Girls like her can't endure things like that! They never can."
And he thought of Sonia.
A breath of fresh air came through the window. The daylight was fading. He picked up his cap and went out.

Of course he couldn't, and wouldn't, consider how sick he was. But all this relentless anxiety and mental torment had to be taking its toll. And if he wasn't actually delirious with fever, it was perhaps only because this constant inner strain was keeping him on his feet and in possession of his faculties. But that artificial energy couldn't last long.

He wandered aimlessly. The sun was setting. A particular kind of misery had begun to weigh on him lately. There was nothing sharp or acute about it; but there was a feeling of permanence about it, of eternity — a foretaste of endless years of this cold, leaden wretchedness, a foretaste of an eternity "on a square yard of space." Toward evening this feeling usually pressed down on him more heavily.

"With this idiotic, purely physical weakness that depends on the sunset or something, you can't help doing something stupid! Next thing you know, you'll go running to Dunya as well as Sonia," he muttered bitterly.
He heard his name called. He turned around. Lebeziatnikov rushed up to him.

"Just imagine — I've been to your room looking for you! She's gone through with her plan and taken the children out! Sofya Semyonovna and I had a terrible time finding them. She's banging on a frying pan and making the children dance. The children are crying. They keep stopping at intersections and in front of shops; a crowd of idiots is running after them. Come on!"
"And Sonia?" Raskolnikov asked anxiously, hurrying after Lebeziatnikov.

"Absolutely frantic. Not Sofya Semyonovna exactly — it's Katerina Ivanovna who's the frantic one, though Sofya Semyonovna is frantic too. But Katerina Ivanovna is completely deranged. I'm telling you, she's totally lost her mind. They'll be taken to the police. You can imagine what that will mean... They're on the canal embankment, near the bridge, not far from Sofya Semyonovna's — quite close."

On the canal embankment, near the bridge and only two houses from where Sonia lived, a crowd had gathered, made up mostly of street children. Katerina Ivanovna's hoarse, broken voice could be heard from the bridge, and it was certainly a strange spectacle likely to attract a street crowd. Katerina Ivanovna, in her old dress with the green shawl, wearing a battered straw hat crushed absurdly to one side, was truly deranged. She was exhausted and gasping for breath. Her wasted, consumptive face looked even more agonized than usual — outdoors, in the sunlight, a consumptive person always looks worse than indoors. But her excitement didn't flag; every minute her agitation grew more intense. She would rush at the children, shout at them, coax them, tell them in front of the crowd how to dance and what to sing, explain why it was necessary, and when they couldn't understand, she'd beat them... Then she'd lunge at the crowd; if she noticed any decently dressed person who stopped to look, she'd immediately appeal to them — look what children "from a genteel, one might say aristocratic, family" had been reduced to. If she heard laughter or jeering, she'd fly at the scoffers and start arguing. Some people laughed, others shook their heads, but everyone was curious at the sight of the madwoman with the terrified children. The frying pan Lebeziatnikov had mentioned wasn't there — at least Raskolnikov didn't see it. Instead of banging on a pan, Katerina Ivanovna clapped her wasted hands whenever she made Lida and Kolya dance and Polenka sing. She tried to sing along herself, but broke off at the second note with a terrible cough, which made her curse in despair and even cry. What enraged her most was the weeping and terror of Kolya and Lida. Some attempt had been made to dress the children up as street performers. The boy wore a turban made of something red and white to look Turkish. There'd been no costume for Lida; she simply wore a red knitted cap — really a nightcap — that had belonged to Marmeladov, decorated with a broken white ostrich feather that had been Katerina Ivanovna's grandmother's and had been kept as a family heirloom. Polenka was in her everyday clothes; she looked at her mother with timid bewilderment and stayed close to her side, hiding her tears. She dimly understood her mother's condition and glanced around uneasily. The street and the crowd terrified her. Sonia followed Katerina Ivanovna, weeping and begging her to come home, but Katerina Ivanovna refused to listen.

"Stop it, Sonia, stop!" she shouted, speaking rapidly, gasping and coughing. "You don't know what you're asking — you're like a child! I've told you I'm not going back to that drunken German. Let everyone in Petersburg see these children begging in the streets, even though their father was an honorable man who served all his life in truth and loyalty, and one might say died in the line of duty." (Katerina Ivanovna had by now invented this fantastic story and thoroughly believed it.) "Let that wretch of a general see! And you're being silly, Sonia — what are we supposed to eat? Tell me that. We've burdened you enough — I won't do it anymore! Ah, Rodion Romanovitch, is that you?" she cried, spotting Raskolnikov and rushing up to him. "Explain to this silly girl that nothing better could be done! Even organ-grinders earn their living, and everyone will see at once that we're different — that we're an honorable, bereaved family reduced to beggary. That general will lose his position, you'll see! We'll perform under his windows every day, and if the Tsar drives by, I'll fall on my knees, push the children forward, and say: 'Protect us, father.' He is the father of the fatherless, he is merciful — he'll protect us, you'll see, and that wretch of a general... Lida, tenez vous droite! Kolya, you'll dance again. Why are you whimpering? Whimpering again! What are you scared of, stupid boy? Lord, what am I to do with them, Rodion Romanovitch? If you only knew how stupid they are! What can you do with such children?"

And she, nearly crying herself — which didn't slow her uninterrupted, rapid torrent of words — pointed at the weeping children. Raskolnikov tried to persuade her to go home, even arguing, hoping to reach her vanity, that it was unseemly for her to wander the streets like an organ-grinder when she was planning to become the headmistress of a boarding school.

"A boarding school! Ha-ha-ha! Castles in the air!" cried Katerina Ivanovna, her laugh dissolving into a cough. "No, Rodion Romanovitch, that dream is over! Everyone has abandoned us!... And that general... You know, Rodion Romanovitch, I threw an inkwell at him — it was sitting in the waiting room by the register where you sign your name. I wrote my name, threw it at him, and ran. Oh, the scoundrels, the scoundrels! But enough of them — now I'll provide for the children myself. I won't grovel before anyone! She's had to bear enough for us!" She pointed at Sonia. "Polenka, how much have we got? Show me! What — only two kopecks? Oh, the miserable wretches! They give us nothing — just chase after us, sticking out their tongues. What's that blockhead laughing at?" She pointed at a man in the crowd. "It's all because Kolya here is so stupid — he drives me mad. What do you want, Polenka? Tell me in French — parlez-moi français! I've taught you, you know some phrases. How else will people see you're from a good family, well-bred children, not like other organ-grinders? We're not putting on a Punch and Judy show in the streets — we're going to sing refined songs... Ah, yes — what shall we sing? You keep distracting me, and we... you see, we've stopped here, Rodion Romanovitch, to find something to sing for money — something Kolya can dance to... Because as you can imagine, our whole performance is improvised... We need to rehearse it properly, and then we'll go to Nevsky Prospect, where there are far more respectable people, and we'll be noticed right away. Lida only knows 'My Village,' and everyone sings that. We need something much more refined... Well, have you thought of anything, Polenka? If only you'd help your mother! My memory's completely gone — otherwise I'd remember something. We certainly can't sing 'A Hussar.' Oh, let's sing something in French — 'Cinq sous.' I've taught it to you. And since it's in French, people will see at once that you're well-born children, and it will be much more touching... We could also sing 'Marlborough s'en va-t-en guerre,' because it's a proper children's song and used as a lullaby in all the best families.

"Marlborough s'en va-t-en guerre, ne sait quand reviendra..." she began singing. "No, better 'Cinq sous.' Now, Kolya — hands on your hips, quickly! And Lida, you keep turning the other way. Polenka and I will sing and clap!
"Cinq sous, cinq sous, pour monter notre ménage."

(Cough-cough-cough!) "Straighten your dress, Polenka — it's slipping off your shoulders," she said, gasping between coughs. "It's especially important now to look nice and genteel, so everyone can see you're well-born children. I said at the time the bodice should be cut longer, two widths wide. It was your doing, Sonia — 'make it shorter,' you said — and now the child looks completely deformed... Why are you all crying again? What's the matter, silly children? Come on, Kolya, start! Hurry up, hurry up! What an insufferable child!
"Cinq sous, cinq sous...
"A policeman again! What do you want?"

A policeman was indeed pushing through the crowd. But at that moment a gentleman in a civilian overcoat — a solid-looking official of about fifty, wearing a medal on his neck (which delighted Katerina Ivanovna and impressed the policeman) — came up and without a word handed her a green three-ruble note. His face wore an expression of genuine sympathy. Katerina Ivanovna accepted it with a polite, even ceremonious bow.

"I thank you, honored sir," she began grandly. "The reasons that have compelled us — take the money, Polenka: you see, there are generous and noble people ready to help a poor gentlewoman in distress. You see, honored sir, these are orphans of a good family — I might even say aristocratic connections — and that wretch of a general sat eating grouse... and stamped his foot when I disturbed him. 'Your Excellency,' I said, 'protect the orphans, for you knew my late husband, Semyon Zakharovitch, and on the very day of his death the vilest scoundrel slandered his only daughter...' That policeman again! Protect me!" she cried to the official. "Why is that policeman coming toward me? We just escaped from one on Meshchanskaya Street. What do you want, you fool?"
"It's not allowed in the streets. You mustn't cause a disturbance."
"It's you who's causing a disturbance! It's the same as if I were playing a barrel organ. What business is it of yours?"
"You need a permit for a barrel organ, and you haven't got one — plus you're collecting a crowd. Where do you live?"
"What — a permit?" wailed Katerina Ivanovna. "I buried my husband today. Why would I need a permit?"
"Please calm down, madam," the official began. "Come along — I'll accompany you... This is no place for you, in the middle of a crowd. You're ill."

"Honored sir, honored sir — you don't know!" screamed Katerina Ivanovna. "We're going to Nevsky Prospect... Sonia! Sonia! Where is she? She's crying too! What's wrong with all of you? Kolya, Lida — where are you going?" she cried in sudden alarm. "Oh, stupid children! Kolya, Lida — where are they running?"

Kolya and Lida, terrified by the crowd and their mother's mad behavior, suddenly seized each other's hands and bolted at the sight of the policeman who wanted to take them somewhere. Weeping and wailing, poor Katerina Ivanovna ran after them. She was a pitiful and awful sight, running along, crying and gasping for breath. Sonia and Polenka chased after them.
"Bring them back, bring them back, Sonia! Oh, stupid, ungrateful children!... Polenka! Catch them!... It's all for your sake..."
She stumbled as she ran and fell.
"She's cut herself — she's bleeding! Oh God!" cried Sonia, bending over her.

Everyone rushed over and crowded around. Raskolnikov and Lebeziatnikov reached her first, followed quickly by the official, and behind him the policeman, who muttered "Damn!" with a wave of impatience, sensing this was going to be trouble.
"Move along! Move along!" he said to the crowd pressing forward.
"She's dying!" someone shouted.
"She's lost her mind," said another.
"Lord have mercy," said a woman, crossing herself. "Did they catch the little ones? They're bringing them back — the older girl has them... Oh, the little rascals!"
When they looked more carefully at Katerina Ivanovna, they saw she hadn't cut herself on a stone, as Sonia had thought — the blood staining the pavement red was coming from her chest.

"I've seen this before," the official murmured to Raskolnikov and Lebeziatnikov. "That's consumption. The blood flows and chokes the patient. I saw the same thing with a relative of mine not long ago... nearly half a liter of blood, all at once... What can be done? She's dying."

"This way, this way — to my room!" Sonia begged. "I live here!... That house — the second one. Come to my place, quickly!" She turned frantically from one person to another. "Send for a doctor! Oh God!"

Thanks to the official's efforts, this plan was carried out, with even the policeman helping to carry Katerina Ivanovna. She was brought to Sonia's room nearly unconscious and laid on the bed. The bleeding continued, but she seemed to be coming around. Raskolnikov, Lebeziatnikov, and the official followed Sonia in, along with the policeman, who first drove back the crowd that had followed all the way to the door. Polenka came in leading Kolya and Lida, who were shaking and crying. Several people came in from the Kapernaumovs' apartment too — the landlord himself, a lame, one-eyed man with a wild thatch of hair and whiskers; his wife, a woman with a permanently terrified expression; and several gaping children. Among them, Svidrigailov suddenly appeared. Raskolnikov looked at him in surprise, not understanding where he'd come from — he hadn't noticed him in the crowd. Talk turned to doctors and priests. The official whispered to Raskolnikov that he thought it was too late for a doctor, but ordered one sent for anyway. Kapernaumov ran to find one himself.

Meanwhile, Katerina Ivanovna had caught her breath. The bleeding stopped for a time. She looked with sick but intent, penetrating eyes at Sonia, who stood pale and trembling, wiping the sweat from her forehead with a handkerchief. At last she asked to be raised up. They propped her into a sitting position on the bed, supporting her on both sides.
"Where are the children?" she asked in a faint voice. "You've brought them, Polenka? Oh, you silly things! Why did you run away... Oh!"
Her parched lips were once more covered with blood. She moved her eyes, looking around the room.
"So this is how you live, Sonia! I've never once been to your room."
She looked at her with suffering.

"We've been your ruin, Sonia. Polenka, Lida, Kolya — come here! Well, here they are, Sonia — take them all! I'm handing them over to you. I've had enough! The party's over." (Cough!) "Lay me down... let me die in peace."
They laid her back on the pillow.
"What — a priest? I don't need one. You don't have a ruble to spare. I have no sins. God must forgive me without that. He knows how I've suffered... And if He won't forgive me, then so be it!"

She sank deeper and deeper into restless delirium. At times she shuddered, turned her eyes from side to side, and recognized everyone for a moment before slipping back into confusion. Her breathing was hoarse and labored; there was a sort of rattle in her throat.

"I said to him, 'Your Excellency...'" she gasped, fighting for every word. "That Amalia Ludwigovna, oh! Lida, Kolya — hands on your hips, quickly! Glissez, glissez! Pas de basque! Tap your heels — be a graceful child!
"Du hast Diamanten und Perlen...
"What next? That's the one to sing.
"Du hast die schönsten Augen, Mädchen, was willst du mehr?
"What an idea! Was willst du mehr? The things this fool invents! Oh yes!
"In the heat of midday, in the vale of Dagestan...

"Oh, how I loved it! I adored that song, Polenka! Your father used to sing it when we were engaged... Oh, those days! Oh, that's what we should sing! How does it go? I've forgotten. Remind me! How did it go?"
She was violently agitated and tried to sit up. At last, in a horribly hoarse, broken voice, she began to sing, shrieking and gasping at every word, with a look of growing terror.
"In the heat of midday!... in the vale!... of Dagestan!... With lead in my breast!..."

"Your Excellency!" she wailed suddenly with a heartrending scream and a flood of tears. "Protect the orphans! You were their father's guest... aristocratic, one might say..." She started, coming back to consciousness, and gazed at everyone with a kind of terror — but immediately recognized Sonia.
"Sonia! Sonia!" she said softly and tenderly, as though surprised to find her there. "Sonia, darling — you're here too?"
They lifted her up again.
"Enough! It's over! Farewell, poor thing! I'm done for! I'm broken!" she cried with bitter despair, and her head fell heavily back on the pillow.

She lost consciousness again, but this time it didn't last long. Her pale, yellow, wasted face fell back, her mouth dropped open, her leg twitched convulsively, she gave one deep, deep sigh — and died.

Sonia fell upon her, threw her arms around her, and lay motionless with her head pressed against the dead woman's wasted chest. Polenka threw herself at her mother's feet, kissing them and weeping violently. Kolya and Lida, though they didn't understand what had happened, sensed something terrible; they clutched each other's little shoulders, stared straight at one another, and simultaneously opened their mouths and began to wail. They were both still in their costumes — one in a turban, the other in the cap with the ostrich feather.
And how had "the certificate of merit" come to be on the bed beside Katerina Ivanovna? It lay there by the pillow; Raskolnikov noticed it.
He walked to the window. Lebeziatnikov hurried over to him.
"She's dead," he said.
"Rodion Romanovitch, I need a word with you," said Svidrigailov, coming up to them.
Lebeziatnikov immediately stepped aside and withdrew discreetly. Svidrigailov drew Raskolnikov further away.

"I'll take care of all the arrangements — the funeral and everything. You know it's a question of money, and as I told you, I have plenty. I'll place those two little ones and Polenka in a good orphanage, and I'll settle fifteen hundred rubles on each of them, to be paid when they come of age — so Sofya Semyonovna won't have to worry about them. And I'll pull her out of the muck too, because she's a good girl, isn't she? So you can tell Avdotya Romanovna that's how I'm spending her ten thousand."
"What's your motive for such generosity?" asked Raskolnikov.

"Oh, you skeptic!" Svidrigailov laughed. "I told you I have no need for that money. Won't you accept that it's simply done out of humanity? After all, she wasn't 'a louse'" — he gestured toward the corner where the dead woman lay — "was she, like some old pawnbroker? Come now, you'll agree — should Luzhin go on living and doing wicked things, or should she die? And if I don't help them, Polenka will end up the same way."

He said this with a kind of playful, sly wink, keeping his eyes fixed on Raskolnikov. Raskolnikov went white and cold, hearing his own words to Sonia thrown back at him. He quickly stepped back and stared wildly at Svidrigailov.
"How do you know?" he whispered, barely able to breathe.
"I lodge here, at Madame Resslich's — right on the other side of the wall. Here's Kapernaumov's place, and next door is Madame Resslich, an old and devoted friend. We're neighbors."
"You?"

"Yes," Svidrigailov continued, shaking with laughter. "I assure you on my honor, dear Rodion Romanovitch, that you've interested me enormously. I told you we'd become friends — I predicted it. Well, here we are. And you'll see what an accommodating person I am. You'll find I'm easy to get along with!"
